hints: Start by picturing the replication fork after helicase has unwound the double helix - you have two exposed template strands waiting for new partners.
Think about how a new free nucleotide becomes part of a growing chain - what type of strong covalent bond links the sugar and phosphate groups together.
Remember that copying must be almost perfect - consider what quality-control job the same enzyme does after adding each base.
walkthrough:
Building on the template**
Each old strand acts as a template. DNA polymerase moves along and brings in free DNA nucleotides, allowing them to line up only if A pairs with T and C pairs with G. This is how the exact sequence is copied.

Joining the backbone together**
Once the correct nucleotide is in place, DNA polymerase catalyses formation of a phosphodiester bond between the deoxyribose sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next. Repeating this builds the continuous sugar-phosphate backbone of the new strand.

Checking for mistakes**
DNA polymerase also proofreads as it goes. If a non-complementary base has been added, it removes it and replaces it with the correct one, so mutations are kept very low.

Final answer: DNA polymerase joins nucleotides to the growing polynucleotide strand by complementary base pairing only; forms phosphodiester bonds to build the sugar-phosphate backbone; proofreads the new strand and repairs mismatched base pairs.

hints: Think about what makes a cancer cell dangerous - how often it copies itself compared with a normal cell.
walkthrough:
Linking replication to division**
Cancer is uncontrolled mitosis. Every division must be preceded by DNA replication in S phase to double the DNA. If replication is blocked, the cell cannot pass through the cycle and cannot divide to form more tumour cells.
Final answer: Stops cell cycle / mitosis / cell division, so cancer cells cannot replicate and increase in number.

hints: Compare the four bases used to build DNA with the four bases used to build mRNA in transcription.
walkthrough:
DNA is not RNA**
DNA uses A, T, C, G. RNA made during transcription uses A, U, C, G - there is no thymine in RNA. The template A in DNA pairs with U in RNA. So stopping the cell making thymine nucleotides starves DNA replication but leaves the supply of uracil for transcription untouched.
Final answer: Thymine is only present in DNA; in transcription uracil replaces thymine in RNA, so lack of thymine nucleotides does not prevent mRNA synthesis.

hints: Look closely at Fig. 6.1 - the nucleus has already divided and the whole cell body is now pinching into two roughly equal halves.
walkthrough:
Reading the micrograph**
You can see one cell constricted in the middle to give two daughter cytoplasmic masses. Nuclear division is complete and the cytoplasm is being split. That final splitting of cytoplasm and cell membrane is cytokinesis.

hints: Think about what chemicals in tobacco smoke actually contact the lining of the airways and what general harmful effect such chemicals have on molecules.
Connect damage to DNA with changes in the genes that normally control when a lung epithelial cell divides.
Follow the consequence through - if control genes are broken, what happens to mitosis rate and the cell population produced.
walkthrough:
Carcinogens reach the lung lining**
Tobacco smoke and tar contain many chemical carcinogens. When inhaled they bathe the epithelial cells of the trachea, bronchus and lungs and can enter the cells and chemically damage DNA.

Mutations in division-control genes**
The damage causes mutations. Particularly important is mutation of proto-oncogenes to active oncogenes that drive division, and switching off of tumour suppressor genes that normally brake division. One mutated cell can then escape normal signals.

Uncontrolled growth**
That cell undergoes uncontrolled mitosis without responding to stop signals, producing a clone of genetically identical, undifferentiated cells - a malignant tumour that can invade and spread.

Final answer: Tobacco smoke / tar contains carcinogens; these cause DNA damage / mutations in lung epithelial cells, e.g. converting proto-oncogenes to oncogenes or inactivating tumour suppressor genes; this leads to uncontrolled mitosis forming a mass of undifferentiated cells.
